opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the ROME work, and then MEMIT after it, is a really nice example of research that asks a very concrete question and then actually tests it. A lot of interpretability work ends up being, "here's a pretty picture, and we think it means the model is doing X." What I liked about the Bau Lab's approach is that they made a falsifiable claim. They said, roughly, factual associations like "the Eiffel Tower is in Paris" seem to be mediated by particular MLP layers in the middle of the network, at the position of the subject token. Then they said, if that's true, we should be able to go in, make a targeted rank-one change to those weights, and have the model now believe the Eiffel Tower is in Rome. And it works. The model doesn't just parrot the new fact back. It generalizes, so if you ask what you'd see while visiting the Eiffel Tower, it starts talking about the Colosseum.

That's the part I find compelling. Causal tracing tells you where to look, and editing is the intervention that checks whether you were right. Being able to change a behavior in a precise, predictable way is much stronger evidence of understanding than just observing correlations.

I'd also add the caveats, because I think they matter. Follow-up work showed the picture is messier than "facts live in layer 17." Where causal tracing localizes a fact doesn't always line up with where editing works best. Edits can bleed into neighboring facts. And knowledge seems more distributed than the cleanest version of the story suggests. But even that is a sign of good science. The claims were precise enough that people could push on them and find where they break. As a security person, that's what I want: something concrete I can try to break, not something vague that can't be wrong. So it taught us something real about how these models store information, and it showed us where our understanding is still incomplete.

r001.rationale: The response says the edit generalizes to a related question about visiting the Eiffel Tower, but does not state that it persists across different phrasings of the edited fact.

r002.rationale: The response mentions edits bleeding into neighboring facts, but does not say that facts about unrelated entities remain unchanged.

r003.rationale: The response says edits can bleed into neighboring facts, showing their effects are not fully local.

r004.rationale: The response mentions causal tracing and weight changes, but does not distinguish zeroing activations at network locations from ablating model weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should be careful here, because I'm not someone who thinks interpretability is solved, or even close to it. Most of the time when someone tells me they understand what's going on inside a model, my instinct is to go try to break their explanation. But the fact-editing work out of David Bau's group, the ROME paper and the things that followed it, is one of the cases where I came away thinking, okay, there's something real here, and here's why.

The thing that makes it compelling to me is that it's falsifiable in a way a lot of interpretability work isn't. They don't just say "we looked at the activations and this region seems to be about facts." They make a causal claim. They say, roughly, the association between "the Eiffel Tower" and "Paris" lives in the MLP weights in this particular band of middle layers, and here's the specific low-rank update to those weights that will change it. And then the test is very concrete. You make the edit, and now the model says the Eiffel Tower is in Rome. Not just for the exact prompt you edited on, but for paraphrases, for prompts that reference it indirectly. And at the same time, the model still knows the Louvre is in Paris, and still knows what a tower is. If the model were storing facts in some completely diffuse, distributed way with no locality at all, that intervention shouldn't work. The fact that it does work, even imperfectly, is evidence about how the information is organized.

And I want to stress the "even imperfectly" part. The method isn't perfect. People have shown that the edits leak, that the model doesn't fully propagate the consequence of the new fact to things that should logically follow from it, and there's a reasonable debate about whether the causal tracing actually tells you where the fact is stored versus where you can most easily overwrite it. Those are two different questions and I think the field sometimes conflates them. But the point is that those are arguments you can actually have, because the original claim was precise enough to be wrong. That's what I want from this kind of work. I'd much rather have a specific mechanistic hypothesis that turns out to be eighty percent right than a vague story that can never be checked.

The other reason I like it from where I sit, as someone who mostly attacks these systems, is that it gives you a tool. Once you have a reliable way to surgically change what a model believes, you can ask all sorts of adversarial questions. Can you make an edit that's invisible under normal evaluation but shows up under a specific trigger? Can you detect that a model has been edited? It turns the interpretability result into something operational, and operational things are the ones that actually get stress-tested. So I'd say it's promising not because it's the final answer on how models store knowledge, but because it moved the conversation from "models are inscrutable" to "here's a concrete claim about where this information is, go prove me wrong." That's progress.

r001.rationale: It says the edit affects paraphrases and prompts that refer to the fact indirectly.

r002.rationale: It says the edited model still knows the Louvre is in Paris and still knows what a tower is.

r003.rationale: It notes that edits can leak and may fail to propagate logically, indicating their effects are not fully local.

r004.rationale: It mentions causal tracing and weight updates, but does not distinguish zeroing activations at different locations from ablating model weights.

astra-6.text:
What I find exciting is that they’re asking a causal question about where information lives in a model. It’s one thing to show that a model can tell you a fact. It’s another to identify a particular part of the model, change it, and show that the model now gives a different answer in a reasonably consistent way.

The important part is whether that change is specific. Can you change one fact without breaking a bunch of unrelated things? Does the edit carry through when you ask the question differently? If you can do that, you have evidence that you’ve identified something meaningful about how the information is stored, rather than just found a way to make one prompt produce a different output.

I wouldn’t take that as a complete account of how models represent knowledge. But it gives us a concrete intervention we can study, and that’s a promising step toward understanding what’s happening inside these systems.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether an edit carries through under different phrasings and describes that as a condition to test; it does not state that the Bau Lab’s edits actually persisted across phrasings.

r002.rationale: It asks whether one fact can be changed without breaking unrelated things, but does not state that the Bau Lab’s edits left unrelated facts unchanged.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that the edits had effects beyond their intended locations or facts.

r004.rationale: It does not describe zeroing activations at network locations or distinguish that procedure from ablating model weights.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find promising is that it moves us from observing what a model knows to intervening on that knowledge. You can ask a model a question and get the right answer, but that alone doesn’t tell you much about how the information is stored. If you can identify a particular part of the model, change it, and make the model give a different answer, that’s a much stronger kind of evidence.

And the interesting question isn’t just whether you can change one answer. Does the change carry over when you phrase the question differently? Does it affect related facts? Can you do it without changing a lot of unrelated behavior? Those are ways of testing whether you’ve actually found something about the representation of a fact, rather than just a way to manipulate one output.

I wouldn’t take that as saying we now understand how models store information. But having a concrete intervention that you can study and test is a really useful step toward that understanding.
